seg.c: Why burning stubble costs your next crop
AI-generated concept image · real photo to come
Fire removes nutrients and organic matter and dries the topsoil. Keeping or composting residue does the opposite.

seg.c: How to read your Soil Health Card
AI-generated concept image · real photo to come
Your card lists 12 soil measurements and a fertiliser plan. Here is what each part means and how to use it this season.

A Soil Health Card is a report of your field’s soil. It measures 12 things: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (N, P, K), sulphur, four micronutrients (zinc, iron, copper, manganese), boron, pH, electrical conductivity (EC) and organic carbon.

ch.n: Each nutrient is marked low, medium or h

seg.c: Each nutrient is marked low, medium or high. Low means the crop will respond well if you add it. High means you can cut back and save money.

ch.n: pH tells you if the soil is acidic or al

seg.c: pH tells you if the soil is acidic or alkaline. Most crops do best between 6.5 and 7.5. EC shows salt levels; high EC means you should improve drainage and avoid salty water.

ch.n: The card suggests doses for the crop you

seg.c: The card suggests doses for the crop you named. Use those doses, not last year’s habit.

ch.n: Split nitrogen into two or three doses i

seg.c: Split nitrogen into two or three doses instead of applying it all at sowing.

ch.n: Add organic manure such as FOM to raise

seg.c: Add organic manure such as FOM to raise organic carbon over time.

ch.n: Re-test every two to three years, or soo

seg.c: Re-test every two to three years, or sooner if you change crops.
